title: Payers are using AI to write coverage policy. Market access teams need to get there first.
summary: AI-drafted payer policies may be finalized before launch, and they can come out more restrictive than intended. That changes when and how market access teams engage.
body: A quiet shift is underway on the payer side. MMIT's 2026 market access outlook notes that health plans increasingly use AI to draft medical policies, evaluate utilization trends, and design formularies and utilization management. Because these models lean on clinical trial inclusion criteria, the resulting policies can end up more restrictive than the payer actually intended.

The timing matters as much as the content. If an AI-assisted policy is drafted before approval, the window to influence it closes earlier than most launch plans assume. MMIT's experts recommend identifying the most influential payers and engaging them well ahead of launch, with access planning starting as early as Phase 1 or 2.

This lands on top of an already tight environment. MMIT data cited in the same piece shows new-to-market blocks rising from roughly half of U.S. covered lives a few years ago to almost two-thirds by 2025. IQVIA's July 2026 market access view adds accumulators, maximizers, and IRA and 340B uncertainty to the list of pressures on net revenue.

What this means for MA&R analytics teams: payer segmentation and policy monitoring can no longer be quarterly exercises. Teams that can quickly compare a draft policy against trial criteria, covered lives, and historical payer behavior will be the ones who shape the outcome rather than react to it.

One caution. Industry research from Day One Strategy finds that AI access in pharma is outpacing real adoption, and that data quality and governance decide whether AI investments pay off. The same holds here: AI-ready payer data (clean hierarchies, current policy text, reliable lives counts) is the foundation, not an afterthought.

title: Drug prior authorization is becoming digital infrastructure. That is a data opportunity for access teams.
summary: CMS's proposed rule on prior authorization for drugs pushes payers toward electronic workflows, faster decisions, and public reporting. The result is a new, structured data stream that access analytics and AI can actually use.
body: In April 2026 CMS proposed its Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs rule. As Fierce Healthcare reported, it would require payers in Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, and ACA exchange plans to decide drug prior authorization requests within 72 hours for standard requests and 24 hours for urgent ones, publicly report approval, denial, and appeal metrics, and move to FHIR-based electronic workflows.

A contributor piece in AJMC frames this well: CMS is shifting from trimming administrative burden to rebuilding prior authorization as digital infrastructure. It extends reform to drugs under both the medical and pharmacy benefit, asks for more specific denial reasons, and notes that contracts signed in 2026 will govern performance during the 2027 compliance period.

The scale explains the urgency. AJMC cites KFF data showing Medicare Advantage insurers made 52.8 million prior authorization determinations in 2024 and denied 7.7%. Meanwhile, MMIT's 2026 outlook expects payers and pharmacies to use AI to reduce administrative work and speed prior authorization reviews.

Put those together and the picture changes for manufacturers. Prior authorization has been one of the least visible steps in the patient journey, usually seen through hub data, field anecdotes, and lagging claims. Standardized electronic transactions, deadlines, and published payer metrics create a cleaner, more consistent signal about where and why patients get stuck.

What it means for MA&R analytics teams: start building the baseline now. Map turnaround and denial patterns by payer and benefit type, connect them to payer hierarchy and covered lives, and line them up with patient services and specialty pharmacy data. When the reporting arrives, the teams with a clean baseline will be the ones who can tell real access improvement from noise, and who are ready to put AI on top of data that finally holds together.

title: HTA bodies have not banned AI in evidence dossiers. They have made it auditable.
summary: NICE, the EU HTA Coordination Group and Canada's Drug Agency now share one expectation for AI in evidence submissions: disclose it, keep a human accountable, and show the validation. For MA&R teams, that turns AI use into a documentation and governance job.
body: Over the past two years, the rules for using AI in health technology assessment submissions have taken shape, and they point the same way. None of the major bodies prohibits AI. Each one makes the manufacturer answerable for it. An October analysis from Eularis made exactly that point in its headline: nobody has banned AI in HTA submissions, but everybody has made you answerable for it.

NICE set the template in its August 2024 position statement. Declare any AI use and explain why it was chosen. Keep a capable person in the loop. Validate the method and report risks such as bias. NICE also asks that established, more explainable methods come first, with less transparent approaches presented as supplementary.

The EU followed. On 15 July 2026 the HTA Coordination Group adopted general principles for AI use in Joint Clinical Assessment dossiers. As Cytel summarizes them, developers stay fully responsible for the evidence and conclusions, no step should be fully automated, and each meaningful AI use must be documented with the tool, version, developer and purpose. Prompts should be retained and available on request. In Canada, Smart & Biggar reports that Canada's Drug Agency issued guidance in July 2026 on AI methods used to extract variables from unstructured data for real-world evidence. It says AI should be used only when clearly justified and should not yet replace well-established approaches.

The practical message is that the burden has moved from the method to the record. An AI-assisted literature screen or an extraction table is acceptable only if you can show what the tool did, who checked it, and how it was validated. That record has to exist before the dossier is written. It cannot be rebuilt afterwards.

For MA&R analytics teams, this is a data governance task. Treat AI-assisted evidence work like any other controlled data pipeline: version the tools, log prompts and outputs, capture human review sign-offs, and store validation results next to the analysis. The same discipline will strengthen US payer value dossiers, even where no rule requires it yet. Teams that build the audit trail now will move faster as JCA scope expands to orphan medicines in January 2028.

title: AI agents are reaching field access teams. Governance has not caught up.
summary: AI agents built for field reimbursement work are now on the market, while most pharma companies still lack fully operational AI governance. MA&R analytics should set the data and oversight rules before the agents start talking to provider offices.
body: Field reimbursement work is starting to get its own AI agents. On October 7, Fierce Healthcare reported that Infinitus launched a suite of AI agents for pharma sales reps and field reimbursement managers. On the access side, the agents answer questions about prior authorization status, claims and reimbursement, and help onboard provider offices with approved access materials. The company frames it as augmenting field teams, not replacing them. Fierce notes there are no performance metrics, pricing or named customers yet.

The direction matters more than any one vendor. Field access teams sit where payer rules meet the provider office. The questions they handle every day, such as where a PA stands or why a claim was denied, depend on data that already flows through hubs, specialty pharmacies and payer portals. An agent that answers those questions is only as good as that data and the rules around it.

That is where the industry still looks thin. ZS's 2027 CDIO Outlook Survey, released October 6, found that 56% of respondents report measurable AI outcomes in commercial sales and marketing, up from 47% a year earlier. But 55% of organizations are still defining or rolling out AI governance, and only 17% say it is fully operational enterprise-wide. ZS also found that 72% of its "AI value leaders" rank data for AI as mission-critical, versus 46% of other organizations.

Put those together and the risk is clear. Agents that talk to provider offices about coverage and reimbursement are a compliance-sensitive use case. If governance lags deployment, the first problems will show up as inconsistent answers, unclear escalation paths and interaction records no one can audit.

What it means for MA&R analytics teams: get ahead of the field. Define the source of truth for PA and claim status before an agent starts quoting it. Agree on what an agent may say, when it hands off to a person, and how every interaction is logged. Plan to measure outcomes such as time to therapy and abandonment, not just call volume. If analytics does not set those rules, the vendor contract will.

title: 340B is becoming a claim-level data problem. Access analytics teams should build for it now.
summary: HRSA approved 10 manufacturers for its revised 340B rebate pilot and CMS opened a Part D 340B claims repository on the same day. Both run on claim-level data, and the timelines make automated, auditable matching a requirement.
body: On October 1, two federal 340B data efforts moved forward on the same day. HRSA approved 10 manufacturers for its revised 340B Rebate Model Pilot, set to begin January 1, 2027, according to AHA News. CMS opened its Medicare Part D 340B claims repository for voluntary submissions. The AHA says it is considering all available options to stop the pilot, so legal risk has not gone away.

The common thread is claim-level data. Epstein Becker Green's summary of the HRSA notice lists 11 required pharmacy claim fields and, new this year, 12 medical claim fields. Covered entities submit within 45 days of dispense, and manufacturers must pay or deny a rebate within 10 calendar days of a complete submission. CMS describes its repository as a test of whether covered-entity data can reliably identify 340B units to exclude from Part D inflation rebate calculations. Testing data will not be used for that purpose yet.

A 10-day clock leaves little room for manual review. Matching submitted claims to rebate invoices, catching duplicates, and making a pay-or-deny call at that pace will push teams toward automated matching and anomaly detection. IntegriChain argues manufacturers need consistent duplicate discount logic across Medicaid, commercial, and Medicare, with 340B claim validation built into the rebate cycle rather than run after it.

The catch is that every denial will be challenged. Hospitals are already contesting the model in public and in court. Any automated or AI-assisted matching has to be documented, reproducible, and easy to explain to a covered entity or a regulator. A model score on its own is not a defensible reason to deny a rebate.

What it means for MA&R analytics teams: treat 340B claims as a core data asset, not a side file owned by contracting. Build one claim-level foundation that joins 340B submissions to Medicaid, commercial, and Medicare rebate data, with NDC-11 and pharmacy identifiers mastered. Start with clear matching rules, add machine learning only where it lifts match rates and can be audited, and report the gross-to-net impact by channel. That work pays off whether or not the pilot survives.
